entities.name: University of Paris (Sorbonne)
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The University of Paris (founded c. 1150-1200 CE, formally chartered 1215), the mother of all Western universities and the institution where Scholasticism — the intellectual tradition that synthesized Christian theology with Aristotelian philosophy — was forged, produced Thomas Aquinas, Peter Abelard, Roger Bacon, and Albert the Great, and operated for 800 years until Charles de Gaulle dissolved it in 1970 after the May 1968 student revolt, splitting it into 13 separate universities. The Paris model — masters' guilds, faculty autonomy, disputatio method — was the blueprint for all European universities.

The University of Paris emerged from the cathedral schools of Notre-Dame de Paris; Peter Abelard's 12th-century lectures (and his love affair with Héloïse d'Argenteuil) catalyzed the university's informal founding. The 1215 papal charter by Pope Innocent III's legate Robert de Courçon established the university's formal constitution: four faculties (Arts, Theology, Canon Law, Medicine), the right of masters to strike (first recorded academic strike, 1229-1231), and the concept of universitas (corporation of scholars).

Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologica (completed at Paris) and the Condemnations of 1277 (which paradoxically stimulated empirical inquiry by banning certain Aristotelian propositions) shaped European intellectual history for 400 years. The University was dissolved by de Gaulle after the May 1968 uprising (when Sorbonne students catalyzed a general strike of 10 million French workers), split into 13 Paris universities (Paris I-XIII) that still operate. The name 'Sorbonne' (from Robert de Sorbon's 1257 college of theology) remains synonymous with French academic culture.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The University of Paris — mother of all Western universities, forge of Scholasticism, home of Aquinas and Abelard — shaped European intellectual culture for 800 years, and its 1970 dissolution following the May 1968 student revolt that nearly toppled the French government is the most dramatic institutional death in academic history.
